newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. peace envoy shuttles between Israel, PLO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. peace envoy shuttles between Israel, PLO.

text.p: A U.S. presidential envoy shuttled between Israelis and Palestinians on Friday trying to rescue Middle East peace while in public the two sides stuck to positions that had plunged the region into crisis.

Backed by tanks and helicopters, thousands of Israeli police and soldiers girded for a ninth day of violent West Bank Palestinian protests over Israel's construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
In Hebron, 100 protesters hurled stones at Israeli troops. Witnesses said Palestinian police tried to contain the riot.

The envoy Dennis Ross met chief Palestinian negotiators in Jerusalem on Friday ahead of a meeting with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Foreign Minister David Levy and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.

Israel again demanded an end to violence that climaxed a week ago when a Palestinian suicide bomber killed three women at a Tel Aviv cafe. Israel has accused Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat of giving a tacit "green light" to the bloodshed.

Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said that Ross had apparently spoken with Arafat in Morocco on Thursday about a need to stop attacks. "And we expect results in the field," Bazak told Israel's Channel Two Television.
But Bazak was unyielding on the one issue which has unleashed Palestinian rage, saying: "We will build in Jerusalem because it's our right."
Palestinians want an end to Israel's construction of the settlement of 6,500 homes for Jews on a hilltop which Israelis call Har Homa and the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Arabs view East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in 1967 and annexed, as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

"There is one item on the agenda: the current state of the peace process," Palestinian Saeb Erekat told Reuters before he and fellow peace negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, went into a meeting with Ross.
"If Netanyahu orders the bulldozers to stop, I think the peace process will be on track...Settlement and peace don't go together just as violence and peace don't go together," he said.
Israeli security chiefs warned of a potential surge of unrest climaxing on Sunday -- the annual "Land Day" when Israeli Arabs stage protests against government confiscation of lands.
"We see the next three days, Friday, Saturday and Sunday...as record days for tension," Jerusalem police chief Yair Yitzhaki said.
"I very much hope that political processes next week will perhaps manage to have an effect and that we can expect a drop in the tension," he told Israeli army radio.

U.S. President Bill Clinton said Ross's talks with Arafat were encouraging but he did not elaborate. U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called on Arafat to give a "red light" to stop guerrilla attacks against Israel.

Analysts view the settlement row as at least as tough a test for Ross as a fierce flare-up months ago when, in the wake of gun battles that killed 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis, he brokered Israel's handover of most of Hebron to self-rule.

They said Ross could devise a formula by which Arafat would recommit himself to fight violence and Netanyahu would promise not to take any more unilateral steps such as last week's groundbreaking on the Jewish settlement.
Arafat arrived in Tunis on Friday to brief President Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali on the crisis in the peace process.
Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani said the Palestinian leader will fly immediately after the meeting to Gaza where he is expected to chair a Palestinian Authority cabinet meeting.
On Thursday, Israel's Channel One television unveiled another new settlement, showing film of a small enclave in the West Bank near Ramallah.
Ross said on Wednesday he would return to Washington by the weekend to report to Clinton so "the president can decide what the next proper move should be".
